title: Strength Training Improves Running Economy Durability and Fatigued High-Intensity Performance in Well-Trained Male Runners: A Randomized Control Trial
authors: Zanini M, Folland JP, Wu H, Blagrove RC
population: Well-trained male runners (VO2max 58.6 mL/kg/min, 10 km 39:02), performance-matched and randomised to running-only control or running plus strength
findings: Maximal strength plus plyometric training twice weekly for 10 weeks versus habitual running only (n=14 per group).

RE (oxygen cost) during a 90-min run in the heavy-intensity domain (13.1 +/- 1.4 km/h, 79.7% VO2max) changed -2.1% with strength vs +0.6% in control at 90 min (P=0.04); group-by-time interaction P=0.003.
Time to exhaustion at 95% pre-test VO2max, run straight after the 90-min run, changed +35% with strength vs -8% in control (P=0.004).
A supplementary 10-week program of maximal strength and plyometric training twice weekly was compared with habitual running only.

During a 90-minute run in the heavy-intensity domain (13.1 km/h, 79.7% VO2max), running economy at 90 min changed by -2.1% in the strength group versus +0.6% in controls (P = 0.04; group-by-time interaction P = 0.003).
Time to exhaustion at 95% of pre-test VO2max immediately after the run changed by +35% in the strength group and -8% in controls (interaction P = 0.004).
Authors conclude that adding maximal strength and plyometrics improved running-economy durability and late-run high-intensity capacity.
limitations: Single-sex, small RCT of well-trained runners; one 10-week intervention; durability measured in a 90-min laboratory run, not a race.
implications: For well-trained runners, schedule two strength sessions per week (maximal strength plus plyometrics) in a block of at least 10 weeks ahead of long-race builds.
Do not generalise to the whole population without caution: female and novice runners were not studied.
Prescribe 2 sessions per week of maximal strength plus plyometrics for about 10 weeks; this is the best-supported recent prescription for late-run economy, which matters for marathon and ultra.
Track late-run durability (pace fade, heart rate drift) as an outcome when strength is present, noting that the trial measured oxygen cost and not drift.

verification.notes: Crossref (online 2025-02-28, print 2025 Jul) and PubMed match; numbers match abstract.
